title: Shiva's still gaze
hookLine: the gods send desire to break Shiva's meditation, and one flame from his third eye ends it
carry: trataka: the great yogi's still gaze

cards: High in the Himalaya, Shiva sits in meditation, so still the forest around him goes quiet. The gods need him to wake. A demon named Taraka is crushing the worlds, and only a son of Shiva can stop him.
So they send Kama, the god of desire, with a bow of sugarcane and arrows made of flowers. Spring arrives out of season. The young Parvati comes near with an offering of flowers.

teach.h: A FLAME FROM THE THIRD EYE. KAMA FALLS AS ASH.
teach.b: For a moment, the poet Kalidasa says, Shiva's calm stirs, like the ocean when the moon rises, and his eyes turn toward Parvati's face.
Then he catches himself, looks around for what moved him, and sees Kama with the bow drawn. A flame leaps from the third eye in his forehead, and the god of desire falls as ash.
Hindus know this story from the Shiva Purana and from Kalidasa's Birth of the War God, and it's one reason Shiva is called Mahayogi, the great yogi.
In temple images and home pictures he sits with eyes half closed, gaze steady, untouched by every pull. Hatha yoga calls him Adinatha, the first teacher.
In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, that tradition's best-known manual, trataka is one of six cleansing acts.

teach.h: TRATAKA: A STILL GAZE AT A SMALL MARK.
teach.b: In paraphrase: with a still mind, gaze with fixed eyes at a small mark until tears come. The text says it drives away tandra, the heavy dullness that settles on a mind.
Notice what's being cleaned: not the skin, the attention. The eye spends the day darting from screen to face to sign, and trataka asks it to do one thing and stay.
Many teachers read the Kama story the same way: a mind whose gaze is steady isn't dragged off by every arrow. That isn't a verdict that desire is evil; in the Puranas, Kama is born again.

teach.h: THE YOGI CHOOSES WHERE TO LOOK.
teach.b: But the yogi chooses where to look. A word of care: never gaze at the sun, and blink when the eyes ask. The tears are a sign of the held gaze, not a goal.

how: Practitioners of hatha yoga do trataka by gazing steadily at a small point, often a candle flame or a shrine lamp at eye level, then closing the eyes to rest; many Hindus picture Shiva, the great yogi, seated with this kind of steady gaze. Teachers advise against gazing at the sun.

the text says a small mark or point; a candle flame is one of the marks practitioners now use.

games.q: Kama draws his flower bow at the meditating Shiva, and Shiva's calm stirs. what happens next?
o: he follows the pull and forgets his meditation.
he catches himself, finds the archer, and the third eye burns him.
he gives up yoga for good.
games.why: his calm stirs for a moment, then he looks for what moved him. many teachers read it as the yogi choosing where to look, which is what trataka trains.

practice: If you keep a shrine, sit before its lamp or a picture of Shiva; if not, choose one small point at eye level, a mark on the wall or a candle safely lit, never the sun.
Look at it, not around it, letting the eyes soften and stay, and blink when you need to; this is not a contest. When the eyes tire, close them and rest, then open them and look again.
If your eyes are sore or unwell, simply sit with them closed.

wordCard.voice: Trataka. A still gaze at one small point, until the eyes water. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, one of the six cleansing acts.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: trataka, the steady gaze. One of the six cleansing acts of hatha yoga.
